awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: A Novel Low Cost Intradermal Delivery Platform For Nucleic Acid Vaccines
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a new portable low cost vaccine delivery platform for nucleic acid vaccines, commonly used to treat infectious diseases and cancer. Current vaccines are delivered using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) which are generally considered complex and generally more costly to produce. Furthermore they can exhibit undesirable side effects. These challenges have caused a steady decline in actual adoption despite their demonstrated efficacy. This project aims to develop a new technology to deliver nucleic acid vaccines without LNPs or carriers in general, using a simpler scalable approach leveraging electroporation. If successful, this platform could expand access to vaccine delivery with fewer side effects, improve their tolerability/acceptability, and support ultra-rapid deployment for biosecurity threats, to provide a new delivery method for vaccinations.

 
This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will demonstrate the feasibility of delivering naked nucleic acid vaccines without lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) using a simple handheld pen design. The device delivers electrical pulses through microelectrodes to create temporary pores in skin cells allowing direct vaccine delivery to immune cells without systemic exposure. In this project, the pen will be: 1) optimized in vivo to maximize gene delivery and protein expression by varying electric pulse voltage, duration, and mechanical micro needle configurations and 2) benchmarked for their vaccine delivery effectiveness against an FDA-approved vaccine with the goal of showing superior or comparable immune responses despite eliminating lipid nanoparticles, in a mouse model. These result will demonstrate preclinical feasibility of a novel delivery platform to match LNP efficacy for vaccines while reducing cost, complexity, and side effects compared to existing systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF SBIR Phase I project advanced the development and preclinical validation of Piezopen, a handheld, battery-free, piezoelectric electroporation platform designed to enable localized intracellular delivery of nucleic acids without the use of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Efficient intracellular delivery remains a major challenge in the development of nucleic acid therapeutics. Current delivery approaches frequently rely on complex carrier formulations that can increase manufacturing complexity, cost, cold-chain requirements, and systemic reactogenicity. The objective of this project was to determine whether electroporation could provide a simple, effective alternative for intradermal nucleic acid delivery while maintaining a favorable safety profile. This project focused on nucleic acid vaccine delivery as a representative application for evaluating the broader capabilities of the technology platform.

The project successfully achieved both of its primary technical objectives. First, Piezopen electroporation parameters were systematically optimized in a preclinical mouse model using a luciferase-encoding nucleic acid as a reporter to maximize intracellular delivery and gene expression. The optimized Piezopen delivery protocol achieved a significant increase in gene expression compared with injection without electroporation and produced expression levels comparable to benchmark LNP formulations while maintaining durable expression over a two-week period. These studies established a reproducible protocol for efficient intracellular delivery of nucleic acids using Piezopen.

The second objective evaluated the ability of the optimized Piezopen to deliver a nucleic acid vaccine encoding the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Immune responses generated by Piezopen electroporation were compared with three benchmark LNP formulations representing technologies used in FDA-approved nucleic acid therapeutics and vaccines. Piezopen generated robust antigen-specific antibody responses comparable to the benchmark formulations while demonstrating a lower systemic inflammatory cytokine profile. These findings demonstrate that effective immune responses can be achieved using naked nucleic acids followed by Piezopen electroporation without requiring LNP formulations. Importantly, these results show that efficient intracellular delivery can be achieved without complex carrier formulations. Together, these studies met the project's prespecified technical objectives, establishing the feasibility of the Piezopen platform for localized nucleic acid delivery and supporting the development of simpler, more accessible, and potentially more scalable nucleic acid delivery technologies.

An important scientific outcome of the project was the demonstration that optimal electroporation conditions depend on the intended therapeutic application. The studies showed that delivery parameters producing maximal gene expression were not necessarily the same as those producing optimal vaccine immune responses. This finding provides new insight into how electroporation technologies can be tailored for different nucleic acid applications, including vaccines, therapeutic protein expression, and gene therapies, and establishes a framework for future optimization of localized delivery platforms.

The project resulted in a peer-reviewed publication in PLOS One, making the methods and results broadly available to the research community. The project also established reproducible experimental methods, optimized delivery protocols, and preclinical datasets that may support further research and development of electroporation-based nucleic acid delivery technologies.

More broadly, the project demonstrated that a compact, handheld electroporation device can achieve efficient intracellular delivery without carrier formulations, providing an alternative strategy for localized administration of nucleic acid therapeutics. The knowledge generated through this project advances understanding of electroporation-mediated intracellular delivery, the relationship between gene expression and biological response, and the factors that influence successful intradermal administration of nucleic acids.

Although the Phase I studies focused on nucleic acid vaccines as proof of concept, the underlying technology has potential applications across localized therapeutic protein expression, regenerative medicine, inflammatory disorders, gene therapy, and more. 

Overall, this NSF-supported research demonstrated the feasibility of a novel electroporation-based approach for localized nucleic acid delivery and generated new scientific knowledge regarding application-specific optimization of electroporation technologies. These results establish a strong foundation for continued development of the Piezopen platform to enable simple, safe, affordable, and scalable nucleic acid therapeutics.
